markers.mechanism: German main clauses require the conjugated verb in second position, triggering subject-verb inversion after fronted adverbials; learners transfer this into English.

examples.input: Today go we to the store.
examples.output: Today we are going to the store.

markers.prompt_hint: When an adverbial fronts a sentence and the verb appears before the subject ('Today go we' / 'In 1999 occurred the event'), restore canonical Subject-Verb order.

markers.mechanism: German subordinate clauses place the conjugated verb at the end; learners transfer this into English subordinate clauses.

examples.input: I think that he tired is.
examples.output: I think that he is tired.

markers.prompt_hint: When a subordinate clause ends with a stranded copula or auxiliary ('because I tired am', 'that he home went'), move the verb back into canonical SVO order.

markers.mechanism: German strictly orders adverbials Time-Manner-Place; English defaults Place-Manner-Time.
markers.prompt_hint: When multiple adverbs appear in Time-Manner-Place order, reorder to Place-Manner-Time as English prefers.

markers.mechanism: German 'bekommen' means 'to receive/get'; learners transfer it to its English false cognate 'become' (which means 'to turn into').

examples.input: I became a present for my birthday.
examples.output: I received a present for my birthday.

markers.prompt_hint: When 'become' appears with a concrete object as its complement ('became a present', 'became a letter', 'became help'), replace with 'received' or 'got'. Other German false friends: chef→boss, gift→poison, handy→cell phone, will→want.

markers.mechanism: German 'bis' covers both English 'until' (continuous duration) and 'by' (deadline); learners default to 'until' for both.

examples.input: Please finish the report until Friday.
examples.output: Please finish the report by Friday.

markers.prompt_hint: When 'until' precedes a deadline (until Friday, until 5pm) for a non-continuous action, replace with 'by'. Keep 'until' only for continuous-state contexts (I will be here until Friday).

markers.mechanism: German orthography mandates a comma before subordinating 'dass' (that); learners transfer this into English.

examples.input: I know, that he is here.
examples.output: I know that he is here.

markers.prompt_hint: Remove the comma before complementizer 'that' in restrictive subordinate clauses.

markers.mechanism: German academic prose prefers heavy noun phrases over verb clauses; transferred into English creates bureaucratic-sounding text.

examples.input: The processing of the data took two hours.
examples.output: Processing the data took two hours.

markers.prompt_hint: Convert 'the X-ing of the Y' nominalizations to gerund form ('the processing of the data' → 'processing the data'); break long noun chains into verb-driven prose.

markers.mechanism: German uses simple present for planned future actions; English prefers 'will' or present continuous.

examples.output: Tomorrow I am flying to Berlin.

markers.prompt_hint: When simple present is used with a future-time adverbial (tomorrow, next week, in two days) for a planned action, shift to 'will VERB' or present continuous ('am/is/are VERB-ing').

markers.mechanism: German 'Informationen' is countable; learners transfer plural to English mass noun 'information'.

examples.input: I need some informations about the schedule.
examples.output: I need some information about the schedule.

markers.prompt_hint: Convert plural mass nouns (informations, advices, equipments, knowledges, evidences) to singular.

notes: German typology: Germanic, V2 word order in main clauses, verb-final in subordinates, dense nominalization in academic register, strict comma rules. NLI 2013 ranked German among the most reliably identified L1s due to V2 inversion and orthographic rigidity.
